\begin{thm}[Main]\label{th:main}
 Assume $f\:X\to S$ is projective Zariski locally over $S$, and is flat
with integral geometric fibers.

\tu{(1)} Then $\IPic_{X/S}$ exists, is separated and locally of finite
type over $S$, and represents $\Pic_{(X/S)\et}$.

\tu{(2)} If also $S$ is Noetherian and $X/S$ is projective, then
$\IPic_{X/S}$ is a disjoint union of open
 subschemes, each an increasing union of open quasi-projective
$S$-schemes.
 \end{thm}

\begin{proof}
 By~\cite[(0, 4.5.5), p.~106]{EGAG}, it is a local matter on $S$ to
represent a Zariski sheaf on the category of $S$-schemes.  Moreover, it
is also a local matter on $S$ to prove that an $S$-scheme is separated
and locally of finite type.  Hence, in order to prove (1), we may assume
$S$ is Noetherian and $X/S$ is projective.

Plainly an $S$-scheme is separated if it is a disjoint union of
separated open subschemes, or if it is an increasing union of
separated open subschemes.  Hence (1) follows from (2).

To prove (2), owing to Yoneda's lemma, we may view the category of
schemes as a full subcategory of the category of functors by identifying
a scheme $T$ with its functor of points.  Denote this functor too by $T$
in order to lighten the notation. And say that the functor is a scheme,
as well as that it is representable.  Also, set
 $$P:=\Pic_{(X/S)\et}.$$
  Note $P(T)= \Hom(T,P)$. %% \{\,T\to P\,\}$.

name: withdrawn-reason-census-by-proposition
description: Chasing a retraction by grepping the retracted citation leaves every paraphrase live, including the headline file's own restatement
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When a claim is withdrawn, the pass that fixes it greps the **retracted phrasing**
("not even a Zariski sheaf", the cited line range) and fixes every hit — then
publishes "corrected in every .lean and .tex site". That absolute is routinely
false, because other sites state the *same proposition* in their own words ("is
not a sheaf even Zariski-locally", "is not a sheaf"), which the seeded grep
cannot see.

In AJC this left the withdrawn reason live for nine hours at four sites, two of
them the files a reader opens first: `Jacobian.lean` (the headline file, carrying
both the bad citation *and* the "FALSE" overclaim in one sentence) and
`PicEtSheaf.lean` (asserting it of `relPresheaf` **by name** — the relative
functor, which is the exact distinction the correction turned on).

**Why:** the headline file restates upstream reasons in its own words, so it is
simultaneously the most likely place for a paraphrase and the least likely to
share the retracted string. A fresh-context reviewer independently found a fifth
copy one file over, with *identical* phrasing — so even a phrase-grep would have
caught that one, meaning the real failure was scoping the sweep to the file being
edited.

**How to apply:** after fixing the sites you found, grep the proposition's other
phrasings — drop every qualifier and search the bare claim — before writing "every
site". Open the headline file explicitly. And when a *reason* is withdrawn but the
*conclusion* survives, check the surviving conclusion's strength word too: here
"FALSE" was withdrawn to "unproved with a refutation route mapped out", and the
weaker word had propagated to fewer sites than the reason had.

name: read-the-source-not-the-route-verdict
description: "The docstring's prescription is simply wrong" was a claim about which route we chose, published as a claim about what the obligation needs
metadata:

---

AJC's board recorded a resolved route question: the seam sorry's docstring
prescribed `th:repDiv` + the Altman–Kleiman quotient lemma as its inputs, both
belonging to a route marked `rejected`, so the prescription was "simply wrong" and
the docstring "has been costing every reader who trusted it".

Reading the actual paper settled it the other way. Kleiman's `th:main` states the
seam's clause (1) **verbatim** — representable, separated, locally of finite type,
no rational-point hypothesis — so the clause is a *theorem in the literature* and
only its formalisation is open. And its proof runs exactly the two prescribed
inputs. The original docstring was naming the inputs of the only published proof
of its own statement. (Bonus: `th:repDiv` is the **Hilbert** scheme, not Quot, so
rejecting the Quot row never rejected it.)

**Why:** "route X is rejected" and "the obligation does not need X" are different
propositions, and a board that has just made a choice writes the first while
sounding like the second. The effect is worse than a stale anchor: it retires the
literature's own proof sketch as an error, so nobody prices it, and the chosen
route looks like the only one.

**How to apply:** when a board says a cited input is "wrong" rather than
"not our route", open the reference and read the theorem's own proof before
believing it. Sources live in `references/*-src/`. Distinguish, in writing, "we
chose otherwise" from "that is not needed" — and if two routes exist, say which
was priced and which was not.
